title: Psalm 55: Betrayed by a Friend
summary: The psalmist, terrified and restless, wishes he had wings like a dove to fly away from the violence in his city. His deepest wound is that the attack comes not from an enemy but from a close friend with whom he once walked to the house of God. He calls on God morning, noon, and night, asks God to bring the treacherous down, and urges others to cast their burden on the LORD, who sustains the righteous.
story: Psalm 55 closes the short Maskil group of David's psalms (52 to 55) and is the most personal of them. Psalm 52 dealt with a liar, Psalm 53 with universal corruption, and Psalm 54 with betrayal by strangers; here the betrayer is an intimate friend. The theme of betrayal by a companion runs through Scripture, from Joseph's brothers to Absalom's rebellion against his father David, and on to Judas. The psalm gives words to one of the most disorienting pains a person can face, and holds it before God.
historical:
The heading reads "For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments. A Maskil of David." Unlike Psalms 52 and 54, it names no event. Many readers, ancient and modern, have connected it with Absalom's revolt against David (2 Samuel 15 to 17), when David's trusted counselor Ahithophel joined the rebellion. David fled Jerusalem, and Ahithophel later hanged himself when his advice was rejected (2 Samuel 17:23). The connection is attractive, since the psalm describes violence in the city and betrayal by a close companion, but it remains a suggestion; the psalm does not name the betrayer.

Other scholars place the psalm later, in periods of civil unrest in Jerusalem, or read it as a prayer composed for anyone facing betrayal. Its descriptions of the city (walls patrolled day and night, oppression and deceit in the streets) fit any time when Jerusalem's leaders turned against one another. The mix of first person and address to the friend (verses 13 and 14) suggests a real relationship, whoever the parties were.
cultural:
Sharing a meal or walking together to the temple bound people in covenant-like loyalty in the ancient world. Hospitality and friendship were not casual; they created obligations. To betray someone with whom you had shared "sweet fellowship" and walked to the house of God was a profound violation, which is why verse 20 says the friend "violates his covenant". The city gate and streets were public spaces for trade and justice, so oppression and deceit in the streets meant the city's public life had become corrupt.

Praying morning, noon, and night (verse 17) reflects a pattern of regular prayer. Daniel later prayed three times a day toward Jerusalem (Daniel 6:10), and the practice became part of Jewish devotion. The dove (verse 6) was a common bird in Israel, nesting in cliffs and wild places, and its flight into the wilderness offered an image of escape to a place beyond the reach of human conflict.
literary: The psalm is an individual lament, but it moves restlessly, circling between inner anguish, the city's violence, the friend's betrayal, and prayer. Verses 1 to 8 describe fear and the longing to escape. Verses 9 to 15 turn to the city and the friend, with a sudden direct address to the betrayer in verses 13 and 14. Verses 16 to 23 alternate between trust and judgment, returning to the friend's smooth speech (verse 21) before ending with the call to cast one's burden on the LORD. The images of butter and oil against swords capture the gap between the friend's words and his heart.

outline.t: Terror and the longing to fly away
Violence and deceit in the city
Calling on God morning, noon, and night
Smooth words and a heart of war
Cast your burden on the LORD

doctrines.note: The psalm names the particular pain of betrayal honestly. Fear, horror, and the wish to escape are all spoken to God without apology.
Prayer morning, noon, and night shows persistence. The psalmist does not pray once and wait; he keeps crying out, confident that God hears.

"Cast your burden upon the LORD and He will sustain you" teaches that God carries his people through what they cannot carry. It is not a promise that trouble will vanish but that the righteous will not be finally shaken.

words.note: Yehav, burden, what has been given or allotted to someone. It appears only here in the Hebrew Bible. What life has handed the psalmist, he is told to hand to God.

Berit, covenant. The friend "violates his covenant" in verse 20. Friendship could be sealed by covenant (as with David and Jonathan in 1 Samuel 18:3), and betrayal broke a sacred bond, not merely a personal one.
Yonah, dove. The dove is a picture of gentleness and flight. The psalmist longs for its wings to escape to the wilderness, a longing many who suffer share.

christ: Many readers hear in this psalm the betrayal of Jesus by Judas, one of the twelve, who shared meals with him and then handed him over with a kiss. The New Testament does not quote Psalm 55 directly, though John 13:18 applies the similar Psalm 41:9 (about a close friend who lifted his heel against the psalmist) to Judas. First Peter 5:7 echoes verse 22 in urging believers to cast all their anxiety on God because he cares for them. Jesus himself did not fly away from his betrayal but walked into it, and he gives his people a God who carries their burdens because he has borne the worst of them.

hard.q: How can the psalmist pray that his enemies go down to Sheol alive?
hard.a: Verse 15 is an imprecation, a prayer for God's judgment on the wicked, and it probably echoes the fate of Korah and his followers, whom the earth swallowed alive (Numbers 16:30-33). It is the cry of someone whose life has been betrayed and threatened, asking God to deal with evil. Some interpreters see such prayers as honest expressions that trust God to execute justice rather than taking revenge personally. Others emphasize that Jesus taught love for enemies and prayed for those who crucified him, setting a new pattern. Many Christians pray these psalms as cries against evil itself, trusting God's justice while leaving room for his mercy.

questions: Have you felt the pain of betrayal by someone close to you? How does this psalm give words to that experience?
The psalmist wanted to fly away. When is escape a good choice, and when must we stay and bring the pain to God?
What burden do you need to cast on the LORD right now, and what makes it hard to let go of it?
